::: {.lead}
Today you work like in a lab: you do four experiments in Excel on the sales
of the Sunrise shop and record what you see. These are the sales of the next
week: other numbers than the table of the lesson. Do each experiment when
your teacher shows it. After each step, write your result in its box. At
the end, copy your key results into the table.
:::

## Before you start

- **You need:** a computer with Excel (the desktop app, or Excel on the web
  at `office.com`).
- **Time:** about 40 minutes for the four experiments.
- **Check:** the results are at the end of this worksheet. Look only after
  you try. On the interactive lesson, every step has a check that answers
  at once.

{{< start-files >}}

## Experiment 1 · Sort

**Aim:** put the rows in order, and see that each row moves as a whole.
*(Lesson notes 7.1 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Open `sales-start.xlsx` (click **Enable Editing** if you see it). On the
   sheet **Sales**, click one cell of the table. Choose **Data › Sort**,
   sort by **Total (JD)**, order **Largest to Smallest**, and click OK.

   {{< record "On top: … ; at the bottom: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   On top: the **bag of Wednesday, 48 JD**. At the bottom: the **water of
   Sunday, 9 JD**. Each row moved as a whole: the day and the item stayed
   with their total.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You sort by **Total (JD)**, largest to smallest. What is on top?

   - [x] the bag of Wednesday, 48 JD

     Why: The biggest total. Each row moved as a whole: the day and the item stayed with their total.

   - [ ] the water of Sunday, 9 JD

     Why: That is at the bottom: the smallest total.

   - [ ] the first row of the table, as before

     Why: Sort changes the order of the rows.
   :::

2. Sort again, now by **Day**, order **A to Z**.

   {{< record "The order of the days" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Mon, Sun, Thu, Tue, Wed.** Excel sorts the days as words, by their
   letters, not in the order of the week.
   :::

   ::: {.order}
   Put the days in the order that **Sort A to Z** gives.

   1. Mon
   2. Sun
   3. Thu
   4. Tue
   5. Wed

   Why: Excel sorts the days as words, by their letters, not in the order of the week.
   :::

3. Click the letter **E** at the top of the column (only the column of the
   totals is selected). Click **Sort Largest to Smallest** (Data, the button
   Z→A). Read the message, then click **Cancel**.

   {{< record "What does Excel ask?" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   Excel shows a **Sort Warning**: *Expand the selection* or *Continue with
   the current selection*. With only one column, the totals would move away
   from their days and items, and the table would be wrong. So click one
   cell and sort the whole table.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   Excel shows a **Sort Warning**. Safe or wrong? Sort the ways.

   Safe: each row stays whole
   :   Cancel, click one cell of the table, then sort.

       Why: Excel sorts the whole table.

   :   Expand the selection.

       Why: Excel takes the whole table into the sort.

   Wrong: the totals leave their rows
   :   Continue with the current selection.

       Why: Only the totals move, away from their days and items: the table is wrong.
   :::

## Experiment 2 · Filter

**Aim:** show only the rows that you need, and see that the other rows are
only hidden. *(Lesson notes 7.2 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Click one cell of the table. Choose **Data › Filter**. Click the arrow of
   **Type**, tick only **Paper**, and click OK.

   {{< record "How many rows do you see?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **4 rows**: the pens and the notebooks. The row numbers that you see turn
   blue: Excel shows that some rows are hidden.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="4" unit="rows" hint="Count the rows of pens and notebooks."}
   With only **Paper** ticked, how many rows do you see?

   Why: 4 rows: the pens and the notebooks. The row numbers turn blue: Excel shows that some rows are hidden.
   :::

2. Select the four totals of Paper. Read the status bar at the bottom.

   {{< record "Sum in the status bar" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Sum: 77** (15 + 30 + 12 + 20). The status bar adds only the rows that
   you see.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="77" hint="15 + 30 + 12 + 20."}
   What Sum does the status bar show for the four totals of Paper?

   Why: 15 + 30 + 12 + 20 = 77. The status bar adds only the rows that you see.
   :::

3. Click the arrow of **Type** again and choose **Clear Filter From
   "Type"**.

   {{< record "How many rows now?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **All 10 rows** come back. A filter hides rows; it never deletes them.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You clear the filter. What happens?

   - [x] All 10 rows come back.

     Why: A filter hides rows; it never deletes them.

   - [ ] The six hidden rows are gone.

     Why: Hidden is not deleted.

   - [ ] Only the Paper rows stay.

     Why: Clear Filter shows every row again.
   :::

## Experiment 3 · A colour rule

**Aim:** colour cells by a rule, and see the colour follow the numbers.
*(Lesson notes 7.3 · about 10 minutes)*

1. Select the totals **E2:E11**. Choose **Home › Conditional Formatting ›
   Highlight Cells Rules › Greater Than**, type **20**, choose a colour, and
   click OK.

   {{< record "Cells with the colour: … ; the cell with 20: …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Three cells: 24, 30 and 48.** The total **20** keeps no colour: 20 is
   not greater than 20.
   :::

   ::: {.sort}
   The rule is **Greater Than 20**. Which totals get the colour? Sort them.

   The colour
   :   48

       Why: 48 is greater than 20.

   :   30

       Why: 30 is greater than 20.

   :   24

       Why: 24 is greater than 20.

   No colour
   :   20

       Why: 20 is not greater than 20.

   :   9

       Why: 9 is smaller than 20.
   :::

2. Find the juice of Tuesday (14 JD) and change its total to **22**. Look at
   the cell. Then press **Ctrl + Z**.

   {{< record "What happens to the cell with 22?" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   It **gets the colour by itself**: the rule checks the cells again when a
   number changes. A colour that you add by hand does not do this.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   You change the juice of Tuesday from 14 to 22. What happens to the cell?

   - [x] It gets the colour by itself.

     Why: The rule checks the cells again when a number changes.

   - [ ] Nothing: you must make the rule again.

     Why: A rule works by itself; only a colour that you add by hand does not change.

   - [ ] Every cell loses its colour.

     Why: The other totals did not change.
   :::

3. Select the quantities **D2:D11**. Choose **Home › Conditional Formatting
   › Data Bars** and one colour.

   {{< record "The longest bar: … pieces of …" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **34 pieces of water**, on Wednesday. A data bar shows the size of each
   number, so the biggest quantity is easy to see.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Where is the longest data bar?

   - [x] 34 pieces of water, on Wednesday

     Why: A data bar shows the size of each number: the biggest quantity has the longest bar.

   - [ ] the bag of Wednesday, 48 JD

     Why: 48 JD is a total; the bars are on the quantities, D2:D11.

   - [ ] the first row of the table

     Why: The length follows the number, not the row.
   :::

## Experiment 4 · Charts

**Aim:** make the right chart for each question, with a real title.
*(Lesson notes 7.4 · about 10 minutes)*

1. On the sheet **Types**, select **A1:B4**. Choose **Insert › Recommended
   Charts** and a **Clustered Column** chart. Click *Chart Title* and type a
   real title.

   {{< record "My title; the highest column" lines=2 >}}

   ::: {.check}
   A real title says what the chart shows, for example "Sales by type in
   one week (JD)". The highest column is **Paper (77)**. Columns compare
   amounts.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   Which chart title is a real title?

   - [x] Sales by type in one week (JD)

     Why: It says what the chart shows. The highest column is Paper (77): columns compare amounts.

   - [ ] Chart Title

     Why: That is the empty title that Excel writes.

   - [ ] Chart 1

     Why: It says nothing about the data.
   :::

2. Click the chart. Choose **Chart Design › Change Chart Type › Pie**. Then
   click **+** next to the chart and tick **Data Labels**.

   {{< record "The three labels" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **77, 51 and 72**: the three parts of 200 JD. A pie shows the parts of
   one whole. Paper is the biggest part.
   :::

   ::: {.fill answer="200" unit="JD" hint="Add the three labels."}
   The three labels of the pie are 77, 51 and 72. What is the whole?

   Why: 77 + 51 + 72 = 200 JD. A pie shows the parts of one whole; Paper is the biggest part.
   :::

3. On the sheet **Days**, select **A1:B6** and choose **Insert › Line**.

   {{< record "The highest point of the line" >}}

   ::: {.check}
   **Wednesday, 65 JD.** A line shows a change over time: up on Monday,
   down on Tuesday, up again on Wednesday.
   :::

   ::: {.choice}
   What is the highest point of the line?

   - [x] Wednesday, 65 JD

     Why: A line shows a change over time: up on Monday, down on Tuesday, up again on Wednesday.

   - [ ] Paper, 77 JD

     Why: Paper is a type, on the sheet Types; the line shows the days.

   - [ ] Thursday, the last day

     Why: The last point is not the highest one.
   :::
